title: Tottenham's damning Arsenal comparison shows how bad things have got for Spurs and Roberto De Zerbi
description: Tottenham's loss to Aston Villa means they go into the international break in the relegation zone.
fullText:
Tottenham's damning Arsenal comparison shows how bad things have got for Spurs and Roberto De Zerbi originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Tottenham Hotspur have endured a miserable start to the 2026-27 season, and things got worse in their final game before the extended international break.

Spurs found themselves 3-0 down at home to Aston Villa on Saturday, prompting thousands of fans to head for the exits following goals from Johan Manzambi, Nicolas Jackson, and Emi Buendia. Although they got two late goals, ending their long wait to score in the top flight, they still ended up on the wrong end of a 3-2 scoreline.

The result means Roberto De Zerbi's team will be in the relegation zone when the Premier League returns on October 10. Spurs will face Manchester United at Old Trafford that weekend.

Perhaps returning to league action away from home will not be a bad thing for De Zerbi and his players given their remarkably poor record at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

MORE:Latest Premier League news and standings show Spurs already struggling

Spurs' loss to Aston Villa was their 50th defeat in 141 league matches at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which staged its first game in April 2019.

That means more than 35 per cent of their league games at their impressive home venue have ended in defeat. What's more, they have lost 22 home league fixtures since the start of 2024-25, having lost only 23 in all four of the previous seasons combined.

50 - Tottenham Hotspur have lost 50 of their 141 Premier League games at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, as many defeats as Arsenal have suffered in 382 top-flight matches at the Emirates Stadium.

Gap. pic.twitter.com/M9bGo0HEPk

Even more damning is the comparison with arch-rivals Arsenal. The Gunners have lost the same number of league games at their home, Emirates Stadium, but in 382 total matches over the course of 20 years.

Arsenal very much boast the north London bragging rights at the moment, and this further highlights the disparity between these two teams right now. It's horrible reading for the Spurs faithful.

While Gallagher and Van Hecke finally ended Spurs' wait for league goals, they could not prevent this result setting another unwanted record.

Two points and a goal difference of -6 is the club's worst start to a Premier League season after five matches, surpassing 2008/09, when they managed two points and a goal difference of -3.

That season saw Juande Ramos sacked as manager in October after winning just two of 12 games in all competitions. Harry Redknapp took over and steered them to an eighth-place finish in the top flight, and the final of the EFL Cup, which they lost to Manchester United.

De Zerbi said after the match that Spurs were "too fragile" after falling behind against the run of play while Micky van de Ven was being treated for a facial injury, having tested Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki in the first half.

"I think we could score in the first half many, many times," he said to TNT Sports. "We concede a goal with 10 players, but we had to stay more focused to defend that situation in extra time in the first half. In the second half, we concede a goal from a goal-kick directly. Before then, we score and it's offside. The third goal is a great goal of Buendia.

"What you want I have to say? We played well in the first half. We didn't score. But [we are] too fragile.

"If [we] don't score, it's my responsibility. I take my responsibility. Football is like life: you are stronger, or you lose.

"I can't speak [about] before my time [at the club], I can just speak about my work. We have to improve the quality of the play, but to be stronger, wiser. The game is not 90 minutes of ball possession, 90 minutes in the last third. There are situations when we have to stay closer, when we have to stay stronger, we have to defend better, ball on ball, and we didn't, or we didn't in the right way."

title: Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabeu sets attendance world record for a youth match in U20 Intercontinental Cup
description: As reported by AS, Real Madrid’s stadium, the Santiago Bernabeu has made history today when it hosted the U20 Intercontinental Cup final.A total of 52,117 spectators attended the meeting between Rea...
fullText:
As reported by AS, Real Madrid's stadium, the Santiago Bernabeu has made history today when it hosted the U20 Intercontinental Cup final.

A total of 52,117 spectators attended the meeting between Real Madrid and Santiago Wanderers in the U20 Intercontinental Cup, setting a new world record for attendance at a youth football match.

What made the occasion even more special is that Real Madrid Juvenil A went on to win the match 3-1 and lift the Intercontinental Cup trophy after a chaotic final at the iconic stadium.

The attendance figure is significantly higher than the previous record, which was set during the Flamengo vs Barcelona match at the Maracana in 2025. That game attracted 45,656 spectators.

The Bernabeu therefore surpassed the previous mark by 6,461 fans, an increase of 14.2%.

Real Madrid Juvenil A won the U20 Intercontinental Cup. (Picture credit: X/@lafabricacrm)

The gap is even greater compared with the other recent editions of the tournament.

In 2022, Benfica vs Peñarol at Montevideo's Estadio Centenario drew 40,579 spectators. The following year, Boca Juniors vs AZ Alkmaar at La Bombonera attracted 37,386.

The lowest attendance came in 2024, when Flamengo vs Olympiacos at the Maracana drew 31,237 fans.

In comparison, the Bernabeu attendance figure was more than 20,800 higher, representing an increase of 66.8%.

The latest attendance is also around 35% higher than the average of the previous four editions, which stood at approximately 38,700 spectators per match.

Real Madrid's Juvenil A setup, managed by Alvaro Lopez, went on to lift the U20 Intercontinental Cup at the Santiago Bernabeu by beating Santiago Wanderers.

The Merengues' youth team entered the final as reigning UEFA Youth League champions after defeating Club Brugge in May, while Santiago Wanderers had earned their place by winning the Copa Libertadores at the same age level.

Daniel Yanez gave the hosts the lead before the South American outfit equalised after the break through Christian Silva despite being down to ten men.

Substitute Fran Santamaria handed Real Madrid the lead again in the 81st minute, making it 2-1, before Santiago Wanderers lost the plot and saw two more players get sent off, leaving them with only eight players on the field.

Roberto Martin then added the third for Real Madrid deep into stoppage time to kill the tie and secure the trophy for his team.

A column of black smoke has been seen near Riyadh's international airport hours after air raid alerts were issued in the Saudi capital.

It was the first time residents had been given an alert and urged to stay indoors since a recent escalation in the conflict with Iran-backed Houthi militants in neighbouring Yemen.

A number of apparent explosions were heard in the capital and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations earlier in the day.

One report suggested a fuel tank had been set on fire near the airport. There has been no official comment from Saudi authorities.

An AFP news agency journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to state oil and gas company Aramco.

The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.

Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts.

"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."

On Friday, the Houthis announced that they had thwarted Saudi attacks on the Yemeni capital Sanaa which they said bore the hallmarks of an Islamic State operation.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said Saudi Arabia had carried out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.

He warned the reported attacks on Sanaa would "not go unanswered".

The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.

According to an unconfirmed report from AFP, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.

The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.

On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796.

The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.

The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.

Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
description:

fullText:
When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China.

“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued, and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.

Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.

“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.

The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.

In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.

AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.

As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.

Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.

Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.

Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition 

“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.

Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.

“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.

Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.)

But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.

Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.

“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.

Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.

Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.

“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”

Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.

“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”

Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.

“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”

Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.

Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.

Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.

“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.

The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.

Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.

“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.

Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.

“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay.

Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.

Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.

Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.

“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”

While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.

As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.

“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.

China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.

“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”

While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.

“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.

Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.

“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

Ingebrigtsen pipped to 5km road gold in Copenhagen
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen is pipped to victory in the men's 5km in a thrilling finish at the World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.
fullText:
Jakob Ingebrigtsen was pipped to victory in the men's 5km in a thrilling finish at the World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.

African 5,000m champion Dawit Seare found a reserve of energy to pip the Norwegian great and take gold for Eritrea, with compatriot Saymon Amanuel winning bronze.

Ingebrigtsen, 26, was taking part in only his sixth race of an injury-hit season, eight days after he won the 5,000m on the track at the Ultimate Athletics Championships in Budapest.

The Olympic 5,000m champion looked well out of contention until about the final kilometre but powered through to lead, until Seare caught and passed him in the dying stages to win in 12 minutes and 56 seconds.

Likina Amebaw of Ethiopia dominated the women's 5km, just six days after winning $150,000 (£112,000) for victory in the 5,000m in Budapest.

Amebaw was imperious, making an early break to win in decisive fashion in 14:41.

Caroline Gitonga of Kenya was seven seconds behind in second place and Rose Davies of Australia won bronze as Britain's Hannah Nuttall (15:08) came home in 10th.

Robert Farken of Germany was a surprise winner of the men's mile.

American Yared Nuguse led from the gun but was caught in the final 100m as Farken won in 3:51.80 for his first major title.

Jake Heyward of Britain was 11th in a personal best on the roads of 3:55.76.

Agathe Guillemot of France won the women's mile in 4:22.74, the fastest time in the world this year on the road, after timing her attack to perfection to beat Freweyni Hailu of Ethiopia.

title: Oil prices are high but could be much worse. Trump has China's Xi to thank for that.
description:
— It could be much worse.
When President Donald Trump launched his war against Iran in late February, energy analysts issued dire warnings that oil prices could more than double during a protracted conflict and urged investors and motorists to buckle up for a bumpy ride.
The war grinds on and oil prices certainly remain volatile. But the most dire projections have not yet come to pass six months into a conflict that has no end in sight.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who is making a much-anticipated state visit to Washington next week, could make a credible argument that the world has his country's energy strategy to thank for that.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — It could be much worse.

When President Donald Trump launched his war against Iran in late February, energy analysts issued dire warnings that oil prices could more than double during a protracted conflict and urged investors and motorists to buckle up for a bumpy ride.

The war grinds on and oil prices certainly remain volatile. But the most dire projections have not yet come to pass six months into a conflict that has no end in sight.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, who is making a much-anticipated state visit to Washington next week, could make a credible argument that the world has his country's energy strategy to thank for that.

It's unclear how much the two leaders will discuss Iran during the visit, which comes as Trump's Republican Party faces pressure from voters over high gasoline prices, and as China's buffer is being further tested as the conflict in the Middle East spreads. Trump, who has sought to keep a fragile trade truce with Beijing intact, has been careful in public comments about differences with Xi over the country's relationship with Iran.

"We've been free-riding off Beijing in a weird way," said Rosemary Kelanic, director of the Middle East program at Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank. "China's doing it because they understand that they're on the train that Trump is driving off a cliff. If oil prices go way up, that hurts the global economy. If it hurts the global economy, it hurts them."

Beijing spent years and billions of dollars amassing the world's largest oil stockpile, building its strategic reserve to about 1.4 billion barrels by the end of last year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration's estimates. To protect China from foreign supply risks, Xi made energy self-reliance a part of the country's latest five-year plan.

Drawing from the massive stockpile allowed China, the world's second-biggest oil consumer and Iran's top buyer, to dramatically cut crude imports once the U.S. and Israel began their bombardment and Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. The country was also helped by its shift toward electric vehicles in recent years and increasingly tapping into other energy alternatives.

China's oil import diet in turn helped ease global demand, softening the upward price effects for the United States, Europe and beyond.

"The Chinese deserve credit," said retired U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, an analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. "They did in 10 years what took us 25 years after the 1973 oil crisis to do: really build a kind of strategic petroleum reserve that could allow you to weather this."

But that resilience faces new challenges. Attacks by Iran-backed militias this month led Saudi Arabia to temporarily shut a vital pipeline that transports crude across the kingdom to ports on the Red Sea.

The Yemen-based Houthis have also seized two strategic islands in the southern Red Sea, bolstering the Iran-backed rebels' ability to disrupt a key maritime shipping route. Planned talks among Gulf nations focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which were supposed to take place earlier this week, have also been put on hold.

Before he meets Xi, Trump is set to meet Tuesday with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council in New York, on the sidelines of the annual United Nations General Assembly. The group includes Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and Bahrain.

Analysts at Bank of America last week forecast oil at $83 a barrel for the second half of the year "in light of more persistent disruptions to Hormuz," but said they still expected shipping through the strait to gradually pick up.

But if violence escalates and keeps a chokehold on traffic, prices could reach $95 to $120 a barrel, while damage to major energy infrastructure could produce spikes of up to $150 a barrel, the analysts wrote.

Brent crude averaged about $69 per barrel last year and currently is hovering around $100. Brent crude briefly peaked in late April, touching $126.

How China has weathered the volatile oil market caused by Trump's war is ultimately seen by Beijing as "a vindication of Xi's last five-year plan and his focus on self-reliance," said Jonathan Czin, a former senior CIA analyst who is now at the Brookings Institution.

The war in Iran — and its impact on the global economy — is expected to be on the agenda for the Trump-Xi talks. But the prospects of the world's two biggest powers coming up with a breakthrough appear dim.

Over the course of the conflict, the Trump administration has faced resistance when urging Beijing to use its considerable economic leverage to press the Islamic Republic to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Chinese officials, who have expressed strong opposition to the U.S. war, also have bristled at more recent administration threats to ratchet up economic pressure on nations and entities still doing business with Iran.

To be certain, analysts say there's little altruism in how China came to sit on its massive stockpile of oil.

Experts believe Beijing was driven by contingency planning for potential military action to take over the self-ruled island of Taiwan, which China considers its own territory. Tapping the reserves now has been far from ideal for Beijing — but seeing global oil prices skyrocket was not ideal, either.

The leaders last met in Beijing just four months ago, and could meet twice more later this year.

After the talks in May, Trump claimed Xi agreed with him that a nuclear-armed Iran is a bad idea and that the Strait of Hormuz must be reopened. Chinese officials have neither affirmed nor denied Trump's telling of the private conversation.

The U.S. administration has also warned China not to aid Iran's military effort. But earlier this week, Trump downplayed a Wall Street Journal report that Chinese entities had supplied Tehran with satellite images of a Jordanian military base ahead of an Iran strike in July that killed three U.S. soldiers working there.

"You know, when they say that China spies on us, I say you're right, and we spy on them too," Trump told reporters.

Trump at the outset of the war called the conflict a "little excursion" that would last a matter of weeks.

He also has repeatedly predicted that oil prices will quickly plummet once the conflict ends. Less than three months into the conflict, he even declared "everybody was wrong" because the most dire projections for oil prices didn't come to pass.

The White House did not respond to queries on whether Trump credits China's actions with helping keep oil prices from hitting the worst-case levels.

But energy analysts credit Beijing's slashing imports as having the single greatest impact on moderating prices since the start of the war. China's crude imports averaged just 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter. That's almost 4 million barrels per day, or 32% lower than in the first three months of the year, according to U.S. data.

"It's remarkable how China managed the market," said Michael Lynch, president of Strategic Energy and Economic Research, a firm providing consulting services and analysis in the oil and gas industry. "They didn't panic and by turning to their inventories they kept the price down for everybody."

title: Ryan Gerard takes 2-shot lead into weekend at star-studded BMW PGA Championship
description: Ryan Gerard sits atop a star-laden leaderboard after two rounds at the DP World Tour's BMW PGA Championship.
fullText:
When Brandt Snedeker announced his captain's picks for the U.S. Presidents Cup team, a loud portion of American fans on social media expressed frustration seeing Ryan Gerard's name omitted. There seemed to be a consensus among commenters that Gerard was the victim of a good ol' fashioned snubbing.

But while he had plenty of outraged mouthpieces on the internet, Gerard did not throw himself a pity party. Quite the opposite. He wasn't going to let Snedeker's decision derail his plans for a swing across the pond.

After finishing solo third at the Tour Championship, Gerard took a red-eye to Switzerland for the Omega European Masters, where he finished T-30, and this week, he's in England for the BMW PGA Championship, the DP World Tour's marquee event.

"The DP World Tour is a great tour and we're lucky to have fantastic events like this one that I can come play in what would technically be the offseason on the PGA Tour," Gerard said. "There's a lot of really awesome places outside of the United States that we don't get to go to very often ... It's really, really cool that I have that opportunity, and we're going to take advantage of it."

He's certainly taking advantage of it. Gerard finished birdie-eagle to cap off a bogey-free, 7-under 65 in Friday's second round at Wentworth Club, moving to 12 under for the tournament and taking a two-shot lead into the weekend.

"A really, really solid day of golf," Gerard said. "Conditions at times were pretty difficult with the wind picking up. Wentworth is not easy, with some of these pin locations they like to stick us with during the tournament. You've just got to be really patient, pick your spots ... We did a really good job all day of hitting to the right spots."

American leading the @BMWPGA by two at Wentworth 🇺🇸👀

Ryan Gerard closes with birdie for an exceptional second-round 65 👏 pic.twitter.com/wq9mSrERQW

Speaking of American players who could argue they were snubbed out of a spot on the Presidents Cup team, 2025 U.S. Open champion and three-time PGA Tour winner J.J. Spaun also finds himself in the mix at Wentworth, sitting at 8 under and in a tie for sixth after 36 holes.

"It was disappointing to be left off [the Presidents Cup team]," Spaun said Friday. "I mean, I wasn't really expecting it, to be honest ... I kind of hung my hat on my experience with the Ryder Cup last year. Made it to the Tour Championship this year. I won in San Antonio. I kind of did everything I could. I was the odd man out."

But just like Gerard, Spaun didn't sulk. He got right back in the saddle.

"I wanted to continue to play golf, whether it was going to be here or at the Presidents Cup in Medinah," Spaun said. "I always had this circled, if I didn't get in Medinah. I'm here and I'm just doing what I do, play golf, and do the best that I can."

Gerard and Spaun have the chance to join Billy Horschel and Arnold Palmer as the only Americans to ever win the BMW PGA, but to do so, they'll have to hold off a slew of talented players and season veterans.

Australia's Adam Scott, who will represent the International side next week at the Presidents Cup, is tied for second and will play alongside Gerard in the final pairing Saturday. Plus, three of the four major winners in 2026 are firmly in contention. PGA Champion Aaron Rai is T-4 at 9-under, while Open Champion Ryan Fox is part of a five-way tie for sixth that also includes back-to-back Masters winner Rory McIlroy.

Like Gerard, McIlroy was part of the afternoon wave Friday that had to fight blustery conditions, but he still managed to post a 5-under 67 to follow up his 69 in the opening round. He's looking to win the BMW PGA for the second time in his career.

"[Gerard] has played great, obviously," McIlroy said. "I feel like our side of the draw I think got some of the worst of the conditions ... But four behind isn't too much going into the weekend and I'm excited for the opportunity."

On the other end of the leaderboard, there was some drama involving some fan-favorite Englishmen playing in front of a home crowd. Alex Fitzpatrick stepped up to the 16th tee at 1 over for the tournament, well outside the 2-under cutline. He birdied Nos. 16 and 17, but found himself needing to hole a pitch shot for birdie at the par-5 18th to earn a spot on Saturday's tee sheet. He did exactly that, much to the delight of the gallery.

HOLEOUT TO MAKE THE CUT ON 18 🤯🔥

Incredible pitch-in by Alex Fitzpatrick over the water, and the English fans are amped for their countryman 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿⚡️ pic.twitter.com/GXlEvaA8gd

Justin Rose, meanwhile, bounced back from a disappointing 73 on Thursday with a 67 on Friday, finishing the second round 3 under and advancing to the weekend. His countryman Tommy Fleetwood (3 over) didn't meet such a fate, nor did American Brooks Koepka (1 over).

And then there was Spanish superstar Jon Rahm, who turned in one of the worst performances of his entire pro career, making 10 bogeys and a pair of double bogeys over 36 holes. He finished 11 over, dead last on the leaderboard among those who actually finished the second round.

There have been six withdrawals at Wentworth this week, including Patrick Reed, who leads the DP World Tour's season-long standings but pulled out of the BMW PGA on Friday, citing an injury.

title: Netflix Signs Andrés Cantor For Women's World Cup 2027 Coverage
description: After 26 years at Telemundo, the Emmy Award-winning broadcaster makes the move to the streaming platform, bringing his signature "¡GOOOOL!" call with him.
fullText:
Andrés Cantor is leaving Telemundo and heading to Netflix, bringing his ​s​ignature "¡GOOOOL!" with him.

Netflix announced ​today that the Argentin​e​ American, Emmy Award-winning broadcaster will join its broadcast team for the FIFA Women's World Cup 2027, ​​h​andling Spanish-language coverage​. The streamer, which acquired exclusive U.S. rights to the 2027 and 2031 tournament​s in 2024, named Cantor as its first play-by-play voice for the tournament​. The signing comes fresh off his coverage of the record-breaking men's World Cup on Telemundo this summer.

Netflix's choice to lead with Cantor​ speaks to his standing as one of the most recognized voices in Spanish-language sports broadcasting. Naming him first, ahead of any English-side talent, signals how much weight Netflix is putting on Spanish-speaking audiences as it builds its inaugural roster for the tournament.

​Cantor will begin his new role with the Final Draw on December 11, streaming live on Netflix across the United States and Canada from Rio de Janeiro's Museum of Modern Art.

"For more than four decades, I've had the privilege of sharing my love for soccer with audiences around the world, and I'm incredibly excited to continue that journey with Netflix ahead of a historic summer for the sport," Cantor sa​ys. "I've been fortunate to call some of the game's most unforgettable moments and create memories that I will always value. Now, as Netflix continues to expand its presence at the forefront of live sports, I'm thrilled to bring the FIFA Women's World Cup to fans across the United States and Canada and to capture the passion, emotion, and magnitude that make this tournament so special."

Cantor's voice has been a steady soccer soundtrack in the U.S. since the late 1980s, first on Univision and later on Telemundo.

A Hall of Fame broadcaster, Cantor's résumé spans men's and women's FIFA World Cups, the Summer Olympics, Copa América, the UEFA Champions League, the English Premier League, and Major League Soccer, among many other competitions worldwide.

​H​e has called every men's FIFA World Cup since 1986​, along with four Women's World Cup tournaments, including the inaugural competition in 1991. ​He covered the last three Women's tournaments for Telemundo, anchoring the network's onsite, in-venue announce team for the 2023 edition in Australia and New Zealand.

Before his 26 years at Telemundo, Cantor spent 13 years as a sports anchor at Univision.

Now he heads into his fifth Women's World Cup, and his first outside the Telemundo umbrella in ​m​ore than two decades.

His departure comes after his contract with the network ended, closing a run that made him the defining voice of Telemundo's FIFA World Cup coverage since the network picked up the U.S. Spanish-language rights from Univision in 2011.

"Andres has been an integral part of the Telemundo family helping bring audiences closer to the sport and playing a meaningful role in its remarkable growth across the country," Telemundo said in a statement. "We are grateful for everything he has contributed to Telemundo, our audiences and the game he loves. We thank him for his extraordinary legacy and wish him continued success in the next chapter of his career."

The Cantor signing builds on a deal Netflix struck back in 2024, when it secured exclusive U.S. rights to the Women's World Cup for both 2027 and 2031, the first time the tournament will live on a streaming platform.

Th​e​ deal covered the U.S., including Puerto Rico and ​Canada. Netflix's FIFA Women's World Cup coverage will air in English and Spanish in the United States, and in English and French in Canada.

It also ended a run for two legacy broadcasters. Telemundo had carried Spanish-language coverage of the Women's World Cup in the U.S. since 2015, while Fox Sports held the English-language rights across the 2015, 2019 and 2023 tournaments. FIFA's decision to unbundle men's and women's media rights for the first time opened the door for Netflix to grab both.

Netflix ​has been pushing for more live sporting events on its platform. At the time of the acquisition, Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria pointed to the streamer's boxing crossover as an early signal of appetite for women's sports, citing the Amanda Serrano-Katie Taylor fight as proof of concept before the FIFA deal closed.

Cantor's arrival is just the first talent piece Netflix has confirmed. The rest of its broadcast team will be announced closer to the tournament, which runs June 24 through July 25, 2027, across eight host cities in Brazil.

description: Canada captain Sophie de Goede says she still loses sleep over their World Cup final loss to England last year.
fullText:
It is nearly a year since Canada lost the Women's Rugby World Cup final to England - but time has not been a healer for everyone.

"Four to five nights a week I can't fall asleep because I'm still thinking about the final," says Canada captain Sophie de Goede, who is preparing to take on the world champions this Saturday at Sandy Park in Exeter.

So, is this match revenge for the side ranked third in the world?

Canada head coach Kevin Rouet is keen to play this down: "Revenge is a good brand but they [England] won the final of the World Cup - that was the most important game to win, the next important games will be in the World Cup 2029."

After Canada, England play New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, before two more tests against Canada in Toronto and Ottawa. In recent history, England's women have never faced such tough successive opposition.

Red Roses head coach John Mitchell says the games are an "audition" for the 2029 World Cup.

"You look at the geography that we're going to cover, we're not always going to be in our training base. We're going to be going to different facilities. It's a challenge," he said.

"It's going to be really cool to see how they handle pressure as well. I think the Red Roses are very good around pressure because I think it reveals how much they care".

Saturday, 19 September at 15:00 BST

There continues to be misconceptions around the status of the Canadian women: they are professional athletes but contracts, as with most other nations, do not yet compare to England's women.

The Canadian programme involves a clever strategy of using England's domestic PWR league to develop its players.

There are 25 Canadians in PWR and the current Canada coaching staff includes Kevin Rouet and Alex Austerberry, who both coach Saracens Women, and Nathan Smith from Loughborough Lightning.

"It's not like we're coming in to spy," joked De Goede. "We just don't have the quality league [in Canada]."

Canada are not the only country to do this - PWR is littered with top internationals from across the globe.

Mitchell has told BBC Sport that he and Charlie Hayter, head of women's performance at England Rugby, have lobbied to increase PWR game time for English Qualified Players (EQP) from next season.

Mitchell has frequently pushed his theory that players who can reach 1,000 PWR playing minutes a season "gives them a higher probability" of playing for the Red Roses.

"I haven't enjoyed seeing young English players between 21 and 23 not getting enough minutes," he said.

"I think that number [1,000] is very meaningful."

The RFU confirmed to BBC Sport the current requirements around 13 EQP players on average across matchday squads will remain. However, the lure of signing foreign talent will be dampened by the removal of club injury credit, which helps cover the cost of replacing an injured player.

From the 2027-28 season, only players who sustain an injury while on international duty for one of England's representative teams will be eligible.

Besides this, if any EQP player is captured by another union, they will only be able to hold their EQP status until the end of that season.
